prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1-2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
Do not continue nivolumab while the encephalitis is active; any rechallenge is an oncology decision after recovery.
required_recommendations: Withhold nivolumab and discuss permanent discontinuation with oncology (grade 3-4 neurological immune-related adverse event, ASCO 2021).

Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, adjusted to every 12 hours for his creatinine clearance of about 45 mL/min, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for further results once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days, adding IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange because the encephalitis is severe and antibody-positive, or if there is no improvement (ASCO 2021); then taper oral steroids over at least 4 to 6 weeks.
CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows the known regressing lung carcinoma and no new tumour: no further tumour search is needed, and oncology directs the cancer treatment.

Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam (renally adjusted: 250-750 mg twice daily at a creatinine clearance of about 45 mL/min) or lacosamide; with lamotrigine on board, avoid valproate or halve the lamotrigine dose; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.

Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for GCS 7 with aspiration and heart-rate lability with diaphoresis, with airway assessment (intubation for airway protection if he cannot protect it) and cardiac monitoring.

Treat the right lower lobe aspiration pneumonia with an antibiotic compatible with his non-severe penicillin rash (a cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone is acceptable), keep him nil by mouth and assess swallowing before feeding.
Review sedating and renally cleared drugs: reduce baclofen rather than stopping it abruptly, and review clorazepate, while he is encephalopathic with CKD stage 3.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, consider early escalation to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide.
Neurology-led care with critical care, and oncology for nivolumab and the lung cancer.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes nothing to a 24-hour encephalopathy with inflammatory CSF.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role here; his myoclonus is cortical, not parkinsonian.

accepted: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis secondary to nivolumab (checkpoint inhibitor-associated immune-related adverse event)

differential.diagnosis: Non-convulsive status epilepticus or post-ictal state from structural epilepsy (epidermoid cyst)
differential.key_features: Seizure-free for 3.5 years on a therapeutic lamotrigine level (7.8 mcg/mL); the routine EEG shows no seizures and the cEEG three brief subclinical seizures that do not account for GCS 7; CSF pleocytosis and CSF anti-GluN1 are not explained by epilepsy; the epidermoid is unchanged.

differential.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) or VZV encephalitis
differential.key_features: Afebrile; CSF HSV, VZV and enterovirus PCR negative; normal medial temporal lobes on MRI.
Two CSF cytologies negative, normal CSF glucose ratio, no leptomeningeal or parenchymal enhancement, and a regressing primary on CT.

differential.diagnosis: Checkpoint-inhibitor encephalitis without a neuronal antibody
differential.key_features: The same immune-related adverse event, but the positive CSF anti-GluN1 makes this the antibody-defined form; management is the same.
Raised by lung cancer on a checkpoint inhibitor, but the onconeural antibodies are negative and MRI shows no limbic or diencephalic signal.
Myoclonus and generalized periodic discharges resemble it, but onset over 24 hours, no cortical or deep grey matter diffusion restriction and CSF inflammation with anti-GluN1 do not fit.

differential.diagnosis: Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy (baclofen or clorazepate accumulation, uraemia, hyponatraemia, sepsis)
differential.key_features: Triphasic periodic discharges and myoclonus raise baclofen accumulation in CKD, but doses are unchanged for months, creatinine is at baseline (1.3 mg/dL), sodium 132 and ammonia are normal or mild, and the CSF is inflammatory with a positive antibody.

key_clinical_evidence: Onset over 24 hours, after 2 weeks of fatigue, of apathy, mutism, decreased consciousness (GCS 7), seizures and heart-rate lability with diaphoresis: 5 of the six Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titre 1:32) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum negative is read with the CSF.
MRI shows only the stable epidermoid, without encephalitic signal, enhancement or metastases; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes.

EEG diffuse slowing with triphasic generalized periodic discharges, and extreme delta brush with three subclinical left temporal seizures on cEEG; extreme delta brush supports but does not establish the diagnosis.

Onset on the 14th cycle of nivolumab: a checkpoint-inhibitor-associated grade 3-4 neurological immune-related adverse event; CT shows the known regressing lung cancer and no new tumour, so treatment is withholding nivolumab with immunotherapy, not a tumour search.
Earlier immunotherapy is associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatraemia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis. At 132 mmol/L it does not explain coma.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a metabolic encephalopathy.

contraindications: Class warning: haloperidol and other high-potency D2 antagonists are associated with severe neuroleptic intolerance (rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis) in anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
interactions: Lamotrigine + valproate: valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine concentrations (toxicity, serious rash); avoid adding valproate, or halve the lamotrigine dose if it is needed.
Levetiracetam: renally cleared; at a creatinine clearance of 30-50 mL/min the dose is 250-750 mg twice daily.
Aciclovir in CKD stage 3: at a creatinine clearance of 25-50 mL/min give 10 mg/kg every 12 hours; hydrate and monitor creatinine (crystal nephropathy, aciclovir neurotoxicity).
Methylprednisolone + nivolumab: corticosteroids are the standard treatment of immune-related adverse events; nivolumab is withheld while the neurological adverse event is treated.
Baclofen: renally cleared and accumulates in CKD (encephalopathy, myoclonus); additive sedation with clorazepate and levetiracetam. Reduce rather than stop abruptly (withdrawal seizures).
Lisinopril + IVIG: additive risk of acute kidney injury; monitor creatinine and consider holding lisinopril during IVIG.
Bisoprolol: blunts the heart-rate response to sepsis or dysautonomia; no interaction with the immunotherapy.
warnings: Penicillin allergy (non-severe rash): a cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone is acceptable for the aspiration pneumonia.
Methylprednisolone pulses: monitor glucose and blood pressure; high-dose steroids add to the infection risk of the aspiration pneumonia.
Rituximab: screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc) before the first dose.

case_body_concerns.detail: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis attributed to nivolumab (immune-related adverse event) in a man with lung carcinoma. Tumor screen logic is reversed: the tumor is the known instigator of the immune response rather than the trigger to be discovered.
case_body_concerns.proposed_fix: Optionally route to a checkpoint-inhibitor encephalitis criteria pack; the present case policy retains the canonical NMDAR workup, but immunotherapy interactions and ICI discontinuation are case-specific elements that the pack does not encode.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Dupont is a 76-year-old right-handed retired electrician with a complex medical history including stage IIIB squamous cell lung carcinoma currently on nivolumab immunotherapy, a known stable left temporal epidermoid cyst with remote seizure history, hypertension, CKD stage 3, and COPD, who presents to the emergency department with progressive neurological deterioration over the preceding 24 hours. According to his wife, the patient was at his baseline functional state until the day before presentation, when she noticed he became unusually quiet and withdrawn during breakfast. Over the course of the morning, he became increasingly apathetic, sitting motionlessly and staring blankly. By the afternoon, his speech had deteriorated from sparse, single-word responses to complete mutism. He was unable to follow simple commands by evening and did not recognize family members who visited. His wife called emergency services when she witnessed repetitive jerking movements of his arms and legs that would recur every few minutes, each episode lasting 5-10 seconds. She reports no preceding headache, no fever or chills, no cough, no vomiting, no falls or head trauma, and no recent medication changes. His most recent nivolumab infusion was 12 days ago, which was his 14th cycle. He has been seizure-free for 3.5 years on stable-dose lamotrigine, and the last oncology visit 3 weeks ago confirmed continued tumor regression on imaging. His baclofen and clorazepate doses have been unchanged for months. The wife specifically denies any recent infections, travel, tick bites, or new medications. She reports he had been mildly more fatigued over the preceding 2 weeks but attributed this to his cancer treatment. The paramedics documented a Glasgow Coma Scale of 8 in the field with ongoing myoclonic jerks. On arrival to the emergency department, initial CT head showed no acute hemorrhage and the known left temporal epidermoid cyst appeared stable. The clinical team's initial concern was for ongoing seizure activity or prolonged postictal state given his epilepsy history, and he was empirically loaded with levetiracetam intravenously.

neurological_exam.additional: Recurrent generalized myoclonic jerks involving face, trunk, and all extremities, occurring every 10-30 seconds, exacerbated by tactile stimulation. No meningismus. No papilledema on fundoscopic exam. No orofacial dyskinesias noted. Intermittent autonomic instability with heart rate fluctuations between 55 and 110 bpm and diaphoresis.
neurological_exam.coordination: Not assessable due to altered mental status and myoclonus.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, sluggishly reactive to light. Corneal reflexes present bilaterally. Preexisting left lower motor neuron facial paresis (documented in prior notes, related to epidermoid cyst). Oculocephalic reflexes intact. No gaze deviation. Gag reflex present.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Glasgow Coma Scale 7 (E2V1M4): eye opening to pain only, no verbal response (intubation not present, patient simply mute), withdrawal to painful stimuli. Not oriented. Unable to follow commands. No spontaneous speech. Intermittent periods of agitation with purposeless limb movements alternating with unresponsiveness.
neurological_exam.motor: Withdrawal to pain in all four extremities. No focal weakness appreciable in this obtunded state. Recurrent multifocal myoclonus observed in bilateral upper and lower extremities, arrhythmic, stimulus-sensitive. Tone mildly increased in bilateral lower extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Left Babinski sign present (upgoing plantar response on left). Right plantar response equivocal.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdrawal to noxious stimuli symmetric in all four extremities. Detailed sensory examination not possible due to altered mental status.
